description: Names aidd retired, and what replaced each. `aidd upgrade --yes` moves a file that still holds one, and a loader that meets one in an error names the replacement. Add a row for each rename or cut of a key a person writes. A row is never removed.

retired.note: `environments` now says where a push or a merge deploys. Until it lists the default branch, or is `[]` when nothing deploys, a delegated merge there waits for a person. The old `false` is cut. The old `true` is cut only when an environment's `branches` already lists the branch that `delegation.default_branch` names. Otherwise list that branch in an environment, then remove the key, so no config says less than you did.
A date a person must act by is `<action>_due`.
It only ever held `delegate`, the role that answers a delegated ask, so it said nothing a person chose.
An Intent names its own `delivery_team`, so a team no longer lists its Intents. Each listed Intent gets `delivery_team` set to this team when it has none.
The people who answer a team's asks are its `approvers`, as `owners.approvers` names them.

A document type is on unless you disable it with a reason. `warn`, the default, is dropped. `off` becomes `docs.disabled.<type>`, and four types were renamed: analytics to tracking-plan, authz to authz-matrix, compliance to compliance-record, migration to migration-plan.
A setting that lets something run is `allow_*`.
`aidd new` names no team on its own. Set `delivery_team` on an Intent, a slice, or a Spec, or pass `--delivery-team`.
The `money.spend` risk rule owns whether a new paid service asks: set its level under `risks.rules`.
A date an event happens on is `<event>_on`.
Nothing ran its `up`, `down`, or `teardown`: aidd starts no services. Keep them in your own scripts, and name AIDD_WORKTREE there.
`aidd init` wrote it and nothing read it.
The paths facet has one name in project rules and in standards.
A rule is enforced by the `tests` entries you name, so `aidd test` checks it. A command that no `tests` entry holds: add it as an entry, then list its name in `enforced_by`.
A project rule's `requirement_level` says how binding it is (must, should, may), and `level` also names a risk level elsewhere.
aidd keeps "approval" for its two gates, so a waiver is granted.

The writing level `ste-100` is `controlled`, and `ste-80` is `instruction`. Only the key is a name a file reads. A level id in a document's own text is a note to its writer, so aidd leaves it as it is.
It only ever held `standard`, so it said nothing a person chose.
A retry is a fix after a red run. Running one command again is a rerun, as pytest-rerunfailures names it.
The config holds the version of aidd, so a Spec names none.
The `Assisted-by` trailer of each commit says which agent wrote it, so the Spec lists none.
`blocked_by` lists work items, so the role, person, or interface a Spec waits on is `waiting_on`, a name that does not read like it.

Five change types were retired, each for a type and a risk dimension, as the `--change-type` rows say: `deps` is `build`; `infra` is `build`, with `availability` in `risk.dimensions`; and `data`, `security`, and `compliance` are `feat`, the type a Spec takes when none is given, with the dimension of that name in `risk.dimensions`. A person may then pick another type, such as `fix`.
What a change costs to run is part of its risk, which a person approves with the Spec. The mapping moves into `risk` as it is.
A date an event happens on is `<event>_on`.
The date the backfill Spec and its review are due. `review_due` names a date to read something again everywhere else.
The tracking plan, a `docs` entry of type `tracking-plan`, holds an experiment. Write its variants, metric, guardrails, and decision rule there, then remove this key.
A tracker holds labels, so a Spec lists none.
A Spec names the `delivery_team` that does the work, a key of the config's `delivery_teams`.

A Spec lists the work it waits for in `blocked_by`, and a Spec that delivers an Intent names it in `parent`. `blocks` is the other item's `blocked_by`. Cancel a Spec that repeats another (`status: cancelled`), and write a see-also link in the body.
What stays true after release is decided with the risk, so it is part of `risk`.
An instant is `<event>_at`, and the event is named.
One polarity, as `aidd risk --irreversible` and the risk rules say it: `irreversible` is true where `reversible` was false, and a Spec that leaves it out is reversible under either name.
A role of the team is `role:<role>`, and `agent:` names only `agent:<harness>/<model>`. An `agent:<role>` becomes `role:<role>`; any other value stays.
A role of the team is `role:<role>`, and `agent:` names only `agent:<harness>/<model>`. An `agent:<role>` becomes `role:<role>`; any other value stays.
A retry is a fix after a red run. Running one command again is a rerun, as pytest-rerunfailures names it.
A person's decision is `{decision, by, decided_on}`.
The name says what the field asks for: a person's acceptance by hand.
The config holds the version of aidd, so an Intent names none.
The project's glossary, `docs/GLOSSARY.md`, holds the terms every Spec shares, so an Intent holds none. An empty `context` is dropped. Move any text in it to the glossary, then remove this key.
A tracker holds labels, so an Intent lists none.
Under `reaches: flagged` the launch Spec is the last slice of the last phase, so the Intent names none. A `launch` that is the last slice is dropped. Put the launch slice last, then remove this key.
An Intent names the `delivery_team` that does the work, a key of the config's `delivery_teams`.
A slice names its `delivery_team` as an Intent does.

An Intent lists the work it waits for in `blocked_by`, and `blocks` is the other item's `blocked_by`. An `implements`, `duplicates`, or `relates_to` entry has no place in an Intent: cancel an Intent that repeats another (`status: cancelled`), and write a see-also link in the body.
Every Intent lists its slices in `phases`. A single `slices` list becomes one phase, `P1`, named for the Intent's title.
A slice names its `delivery_team` as an Intent does.
Evidence is a runner's exit code on a commit. What a claim rests on is its `basis`.
A proposal names the `delivery_team` accountable for it, as a Spec and an Intent do.
A runbook names the `delivery_team` that keeps it current, as a Spec and an Intent do. With `delivery_teams` in the config, `aidd validate` warns about a name that is none of its keys.
The name is a fact about the runbook, not a verb. `aidd doctor` checks a restore drill only for `restores_data: true`.
A postmortem names the `delivery_team` that owns its review, as a Spec and an Intent do.
Evidence is a runner's exit code on a commit. What a spike's outcome rests on is its `basis`.
The exploration belongs to a role, and `owner` names a person everywhere else.
The note names the role that takes the work next.
A standard's source is a `citation`, the same in the registry and the library: `citation.url` is the page, and `citation.quote` is the sentence read there.
A standard's source is a `citation`, the same in the registry and the library: `citation.url` is the page, and `citation.quote` is the sentence read there.
A versioned file names the version of its shape `schema_version`, a string. A sitemap that says `format: 1` says `schema_version: "1"`. The prototype tool reads both.
An instant is `<event>_at`, and the event is named. A record is history and aidd never rewrites one, so a reader reads the `at` of a record from an older aidd as `recorded_at`.

aidd keeps "approval" for its two gates, so the question type that asks yes or no is `yes_no`. A record from an older aidd says `approval`, and a reader reads it as `yes_no`. A new record never says `approval`.
A runbook, a postmortem, and a proposal name their `delivery_team`, as a Spec and an Intent do. `aidd new` takes one flag for all five.
A compliance change is now the risk dimension `compliance`, which keeps the route major as the type did. Give the change's own type with it, such as `feat` or `fix`.
A data change is now the risk dimension `data`, which keeps the route major as the type did. Give the change's own type with it, such as `feat` or `fix`.
A change to third-party packages is a `build` change, as in Conventional Commits. The `dependencies` area still raises its route.
An infrastructure change is a `build` change that can take a service down, so it declares `availability`, which keeps its route at least normal as the type did.
A security change is now the risk dimension `security`, which keeps the route major as the type did. Give the change's own type with it, such as `feat` or `fix`.
